person.name: Steve_Jobs
person.summary: Steve Jobs was an American entrepreneur and product visionary who co-founded Apple and helped drive major shifts in personal computing, animated film, digital media, and smartphones. After early success with Apple II and the Macintosh, he left Apple to found NeXT and to build Pixar into a groundbreaking animation studio. Returning to Apple in 1997, he led a major corporate and product revival culminating in devices such as the iPod and iPhone, while navigating a long illness in his final years.

chapters.headline: Adopted, Restless, Seeking
chapters.description: Born into one family, claimed by another, Jobs grew up in the Bay Area learning to love the elegance of well-made things—then almost immediately started questioning every inherited script. By Reed and then India, he was already collecting the obsessions—simplicity, mysticism, typography—that would later masquerade as “taste” and harden into doctrine.

chapters.headline: Garage Gospel
chapters.description: In a new industry with no rules, Jobs discovered he could turn engineering into desire and small demos into destiny. As Apple sprinted from a scrappy partnership to a public company, his ambition sharpened—alongside early personal consequences he couldn’t keynote away.

chapters.headline: Macintosh, Boardroom Exile
chapters.description: With the Macintosh, Jobs tried to drag computing into a friendlier future—then collided with the grown-up machinery of power inside the company he created. The result was a public triumph followed by a private defeat: pushed out, he walked away determined to build a world where he could control every detail again.

chapters.headline: Beautiful Failures, Animated Breakthrough
chapters.description: Exiled from Apple, Jobs spent a decade funding conviction: NeXT pursued a pristine computer for the future, while Pixar bet that code could make audiences feel. When Toy Story hit, it didn’t just validate the technology—it proved Jobs could nurture a revolution outside the one that had rejected him.

chapters.headline: Return, Reinvention, Farewell
chapters.description: Jobs came back to a struggling Apple with NeXT’s blueprint and a purist design ally in Jony Ive, then rebuilt the company by fusing hardware, software, and culture into one relentless ecosystem. Even as illness shadowed him, the iPod, iTunes, and iPhone made his second act definitive—until he finally handed the helm to Tim Cook and slipped from the stage.

conclusion: Steve Jobs turned personal obsession into industrial force, repeatedly remaking Apple—and the public’s expectations of technology—through ruthless focus on what “felt” inevitable. His legacy isn’t just a set of products; it’s the modern idea that design, software, and storytelling can fuse into a single, world-shaping experience.

events.date_note: Adopted shortly after birth by Paul and Clara Jobs
events.title: Birth and adoption
events.description: Steven Paul Jobs was born to Joanne Schieble and Abdulfattah Jandali and was adopted soon after by Paul and Clara Jobs. He grew up in the San Francisco Bay Area, where his adoptive father’s mechanical skills and encouragement shaped his early fascination with making things. Jobs later treated his adoptive parents as his parents “1,000%,” while expressing complicated feelings about his biological family.

events.date_note: He left Reed after about one semester, then continued auditing classes such as calligraphy
events.title: Enters and leaves Reed
events.description: Jobs enrolled at Reed College in Oregon but soon dropped out, unwilling to spend his parents’ money on a path he considered aimless. Despite leaving formal enrollment, he remained on campus auditing classes, including calligraphy, that influenced his later emphasis on typography and design. The Reed period also deepened his interest in counterculture ideas and unconventional learning.

images.caption: Steve Jobs in the 1972 Homestead High yearbook

events.title: India spiritual journey
events.description: Jobs traveled through India in 1974 seeking spiritual enlightenment, trekking with [[Daniel Kottke|a Reed College friend]] to visit Neem Karoli Baba’s ashram in [[Kainchi Dham|Kainchi]]; afterward he became deeply interested in Zen Buddhism. These experiences reinforced his attraction to simplicity, focus, and disciplined aesthetics, and the spiritual search became part of the personal mythology he later wove into his leadership style and product philosophy.

Daniel Kottke.explanation: An American businessman and early Apple employee who was a close friend of Jobs; he accompanied Jobs on the 1974 India trip seeking spiritual enlightenment.

Kainchi Dham.explanation: A Hindu ashram and pilgrimage site in Uttarakhand associated with Neem Karoli Baba; Jobs and Kottke traveled there in 1974 hoping to meet him.

events.title: Co-founds Apple
events.description: Jobs co-founded Apple with Steve Wozniak (and briefly Ronald Wayne) on April 1, 1976, to develop and sell personal computers. The venture turned Wozniak’s technical designs into a commercial product and positioned Jobs as a driving force behind product direction, marketing, and ambition. Apple’s early work quickly placed the pair at the center of the emerging personal-computer industry.

events.title: Launches Apple II
events.description: Apple introduced the Apple II, which became one of the first highly successful mass-produced microcomputers. The machine’s popularity brought Apple rapid growth, public attention, and major investment interest. The Apple II era established Jobs as a prominent young figure in Silicon Valley’s personal-computing revolution.

events.title: Lisa is born
events.description: Jobs’s daughter, Lisa, was born to Chrisann Brennan, with whom he had an on-and-off relationship dating back to high school. Jobs initially denied paternity, leading to a prolonged and public dispute that intersected with his growing fame at Apple. Over time, he acknowledged Lisa and their relationship evolved, though it remained complicated.

events.date_note: The key visit is commonly associated with Xerox PARC demonstrations of the Alto and its graphical interface concepts
events.title: Discovers GUI at Xerox
events.description: In 1979, Jobs recognized the commercial potential of Xerox’s mouse-driven [[graphical user interface|graphical user interface]] technology after seeing work at the company’s research center. He pushed Apple toward building GUI-based computers, reshaping the company’s research priorities and product strategy. The decision fed directly into the costly Lisa effort and the later Macintosh breakthrough.

images.caption: Entrance to Xerox PARC in Palo Alto

graphical user interface.explanation: A computer interface that lets users interact through on-screen windows, icons, menus, and a pointer (often controlled by a mouse), rather than typing commands.

events.title: Apple goes public
events.description: Apple’s initial public offering turned Jobs into a multimillionaire and made the company a major corporate force in technology. The IPO also raised expectations for Apple’s next breakthroughs beyond the Apple II line. Jobs’s role shifted further toward high-stakes leadership, product positioning, and internal power struggles.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, United States

images.caption: Apple Computer Inc. IPO prospectus, December 1980

events.title: Unveils Macintosh
events.description: Jobs introduced the [[Macintosh|Macintosh]] as a mass-market computer built around a [[graphical user interface|graphical user interface]] and mouse. The launch became one of the era’s defining technology events and helped redefine how non-specialists could interact with computers. The Macintosh’s later pairing with key software and printing technology helped catalyze the [[desktop publishing|desktop publishing]] industry.

images.caption: Steve Jobs with a Macintosh computer, January 1984

Macintosh.explanation: Apple’s original mass-market personal computer line, first introduced in 1984 and known for popularizing a GUI-driven user experience.

graphical user interface.explanation: A visual way of interacting with a computer using windows, icons, and menus, rather than typing only text commands.

desktop publishing.explanation: Producing professional-looking page layouts on a personal computer, commonly associated with the 1980s rise of the Mac plus software like PageMaker and Apple’s LaserWriter printer.

events.date_note: Jobs resigned in 1985 after losing influence in a boardroom struggle involving CEO John Sculley
events.title: Leaves Apple amid conflict
events.description: After a power struggle with Apple’s board and CEO John Sculley, Jobs departed the company he helped create. The split marked a turning point, ending his first Apple era and forcing him to rebuild influence from outside. The departure also intensified his determination to pursue new platforms and control product direction more directly.

events.title: Founds NeXT
events.description: Jobs founded NeXT, aiming to build advanced computer systems for higher-education and business markets. He recruited talent and brought a premium design-and-engineering approach to a new platform effort. Although NeXT struggled commercially, its software and tools later became central to Jobs’s eventual return to Apple.

images.caption: Entrance view of NeXT Computer Inc.

events.date_note: Jobs bought Lucasfilm’s computer graphics division, later spun off as Pixar, becoming chairman and majority shareholder
events.title: Buys Pixar’s predecessor
events.description: Jobs purchased the computer graphics division of [[Lucasfilm|Lucasfilm]] and oversaw its spin-off as [[Pixar|Pixar]]. He backed the company through years of technical development and business uncertainty, shaping its strategic direction and survival. The move placed him at the intersection of computing and film, expanding his influence beyond hardware.

images.caption: Entrance to Pixar's studio lot in Emeryville, California

Lucasfilm.explanation: American film and television production company founded by George Lucas; its Computer Division’s Graphics Group was sold in 1986 and became the core of Pixar.

Pixar.explanation: Animation studio that originated as Lucasfilm’s Graphics Group; after the 1986 purchase it was spun off as an independent company with Jobs as its owner and board chairman.

events.title: Toy Story debuts
events.description: Pixar released Toy Story, the first feature-length computer-animated film, validating the studio’s technology and creative model. The film’s success transformed Pixar into a leading animation company and strengthened Jobs’s reputation as a builder of new industries. It also set the stage for Pixar’s rise as a long-running hitmaker.

images.caption: Pixar Animation Studios logo used since Toy Story (1995)

events.date_note: Jobs returned after Apple acquired NeXT and soon became CEO (initially as interim CEO)
events.title: Returns to lead Apple
events.description: Jobs returned to Apple after the company acquired NeXT, bringing NeXT’s software foundation and many colleagues with him. He became CEO and focused on stabilizing a company widely seen as near collapse. Working closely with designer Jony Ive, he drove a design-centered revival that began with the “Think different” campaign and products such as the iMac.

events.date_note: This period captures the iPod launch and the subsequent iTunes Store opening as a unified ecosystem shift
events.title: Builds iPod and iTunes
events.description: Apple expanded from computers into consumer electronics and digital media with the iPod and an emerging [[iTunes|iTunes music-software]] strategy. The approach culminated in a broader ecosystem that linked devices, software, and a digital marketplace, strengthening Apple’s business model and cultural reach. These moves repositioned Apple as a leading consumer brand rather than a niche computer company.

iTunes.explanation: Apple’s digital media player and library software, launched in 2001 (initially for Mac), that became the hub for managing music on the iPod and later for purchasing downloads via the iTunes Store.

events.date_note: Jobs was diagnosed in 2003 with a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor; his health problems included major treatment and extended medical leaves before resigning as CEO
events.title: Health crisis and step-down
events.description: In 2003, Jobs was diagnosed with a [[pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor|pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor]], beginning a long period of serious illness that intermittently removed him from day-to-day leadership at Apple. Over subsequent years he took medical leaves while remaining central to major strategic decisions. In 2011 he resigned as Apple’s CEO, formalizing a transition as his health declined and [[Tim Cook|Tim Cook]] became CEO.

pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.explanation: A relatively rare type of pancreatic tumor arising from hormone-producing (neuroendocrine) cells; often distinct from the more common pancreatic adenocarcinoma and may have different prognosis and treatments.

events.title: Introduces iPhone
events.description: Jobs unveiled the iPhone, presenting it as a unified device combining a phone, iPod, and internet communicator. The product shifted expectations for mobile computing through multitouch interaction and integrated software services. Its release helped redefine Apple’s future around smartphones and app-driven platforms.

images.caption: Steve Jobs during his keynote at Macworld Expo 2007

events.date_note: Cause reported as tumor-related respiratory arrest
events.title: Dies at age 56
events.description: Jobs died after years of illness related to [[neuroendocrine tumor|pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor]] cancer. His death marked the end of a career that had repeatedly reshaped Apple and influenced multiple technology and media industries. In his final period, he remained closely associated with Apple’s product culture even as leadership transitioned.

neuroendocrine tumor.explanation: A type of tumor arising from hormone-producing neuroendocrine cells; Steve Jobs was diagnosed with a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, which is distinct from the more common pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
